source: Klahr (1994) Children, Adults, and Machines as Discovery Systems (summary of SDDS)
finding: States the SDDS (Scientific Discovery as Dual Search) framework of Klahr and Dunbar 1988. Discovery is search in two spaces: a hypothesis space (H-space) and an experiment space (E-space), plus operators that map between them and a third step, evaluating evidence by comparing predictions with results.
numbers: Three components: search H-space, search E-space, evaluate evidence. H-space goal state is a hypothesis that accounts for most known facts in a more concise or universal form.
quote: Scientific discovery is a type of problem solving in which search takes place in two quite distinct spaces: an hypotheses space and an experiment space
limits: Secondary summary by the original author, not the 1988 paper itself. Domain is a toy device (BigTrak), not real science.
agent_relevance: Maps to S3 GENERATE (H-space) and S4 TEST (E-space plus evidence evaluation). The schema has one generate/test loop; SDDS says the two spaces are searched separately and bridged.

source: Klahr (1994) summary of Klahr and Dunbar (1988): BigTrak paradigm and first result
finding: Paradigm: subjects learn a programmable toy tank (BigTrak) until all share a criterion, then must discover what a new RPT key does by writing programs. They are never told if they are right and must decide when to stop. CMU undergraduates were compared with children aged 8 to 11. Nearly all children failed but most were sure they had the right rule and stopped satisfied. Nearly all adults found the rule, yet adults did not differ much from children in time, number of hypotheses or number of experiments.
numbers: Adults: nearly all discovered the rule. Children (8-11): nearly all failed; most failed children were confident. Effort measures (time, hypotheses, experiments) similar across groups. Exact counts per group are not in this summary.
limits: Exact N and percentages for the 1988 experiment were not in the text read (the 1988 Wiley PDF returned HTTP 403). Do not quote counts for 1988 from this line.
agent_relevance: Failure was not low effort; it was wrong search control and false confidence. Supports G3 and G10: confidence and stopping need an external check, not the searcher's feeling.

source: Klahr (1994) summary of Klahr and Dunbar (1988): Theorists versus Experimenters
finding: Among adults two strategies appeared. Theorists proposed the correct hypothesis before they had enough evidence to induce it. Experimenters ran experiments with no hypothesis and proposed the correct rule only after the evidence was enough to induce it. SDDS therefore allows experiments run without a clear theory.
numbers: Two adult strategy types, named Theorist and Experimenter. No counts given in this summary.
limits: Type split is descriptive. Dunbar's later work is needed to see if it is stable; not read this session.
agent_relevance: Both routes to a rule are valid. The schema's S2 REPRESENT (study examples, then hypothesise) is the Experimenter route; S3 first is the Theorist route. A fixed order may suit only one type.

source: Klahr, Fay and Dunbar (1993) via Klahr (1994): success by group and plausibility
finding: Subjects got a Given rule that was wrong; the real (Actual) rule was plausible or implausible, and the Given was somewhat wrong (same frame) or very wrong (different frame). Success fell with age and with implausibility of the true rule. No third grader found any implausible rule.
numbers: Actual rule discovered by 83% of CMU undergraduates, 65% of community college students, 53% of 6th graders (mean age 11), 33% of 3rd graders (mean age 9). When the actual rule was implausible: 56% of adults vs 13% of children; 0% of 3rd graders.
limits: Group sizes not given in the summary. Device is BigTrak. Plausibility was set by a frame, so the effect may be partly about knowledge, not only domain-general skill.
agent_relevance: Prior plausibility steers which experiments get run. An LLM's priors work the same way: an implausible true rule is the hard case (see a22 on prior information). The agent needs a way to test implausible hypotheses on purpose.

source: Klahr (1994) summary: four domain-general heuristics for E-space search
finding: Four heuristics found: (1) use the plausibility of the current hypothesis to choose the experimental strategy (confirm or disconfirm); (2) focus on one dimension of an experiment or hypothesis at a time; (3) maintain observability (design runs whose outcome you can read); (4) design experiments that give characteristic results, such as many distinct commands. Adults used all four and could handle their conflicts; children dropped them or let one dominate. Third graders did not try to keep experiments observable; sixth graders and adults did.
numbers: Four heuristics. Third graders vs sixth graders and adults differed on observability.
limits: Heuristic list comes from the 1993 study with four groups; not tested outside BigTrak in this summary.
agent_relevance: Candidate S4 design rules for the agent: change one thing at a time, keep outcomes readable, pick runs with a distinctive signature. These can be checked in code (count variables changed per test).

source: Klahr (1994) summary: gaps in current discovery models
finding: Klahr says two spaces are not enough. A full account needs an instrumentation space, a representation space and a communication space. He also says machine discovery systems assume the data are given and model neither motivation nor social context, and most work uses simplified domains.
numbers: Three extra spaces named: instrumentation, representation, communication. Cites Cheng and Simon 1992 and Kaplan and Simon 1990 for representation search.
limits: Position statement from 1992, not a measured result.
agent_relevance: The representation space matches S2 REPRESENT. The schema has no instrumentation step (choosing what to measure); note it as a gap, and check section 4b before adding anything.

source: Langley (1979) Rediscovering Physics with BACON.3 (IJCAI)
finding: BACON.3 is a production system of about 86 OPS2 rules in seven sets. It finds constancies and trends in data, defines new terms (products and ratios) and builds higher levels of description, so a hypothesis at one level becomes data at the next. It collects data by a factorial design, varying one variable at a time.
numbers: Rediscovered 5 laws: ideal gas, Kepler's third, Coulomb's, Ohm's, Galileo's. Ideal gas path: pV constant at fixed n and T, then pV/T slope 8.32, then pV/nT = 8.32. Productions fired: gas 1203, Kepler 1119, Coulomb 1297, Galileo 1150, Ohm 4593. Defined terms: 8, 17, 18, 9, 31 (redundant terms 2, 1, 12, 7, 84).
limits: Data are clean and the variables are given by the programmer. The paper reports no test on data BACON was not built for. Noise handling is a redefined LISP equal that ignores small differences.
agent_relevance: Gives the E-space side a concrete rule: vary one variable at a time, look for constants, define a ratio or product when a trend appears. These steps can run in code outside the model, which fits the rule that the program decides and the model only fills a slot.

source: Langley (1979) BACON.3: robustness to data order and irrelevant variables
finding: Order of data collection changed the path but not the law. For ideal gas, varying moles first gave V/n, then V/nT, then pV/nT, the same law by another route. For Galileo's pendulum, varying irrelevant variables (weight, angle) first found them irrelevant at once; varying them last reached the same laws with more computation.
numbers: Heuristic use by task (Table 7): 'ignore differences' in 4 tasks, 'collapse descriptions' in 5, 'different experiments' in 2, 'irrelevant variables' in 1. Ohm's law was the most expensive (4593 productions).
limits: Only one reorder per law was tried. No statistics.
agent_relevance: In clean data, variable order changes cost, not outcome. For the agent: test order is a cost lever, not a correctness lever, when a check exists.

source: Wason (1960) 2-4-6 task, as described and counted by Jhaveri et al. (2026)
finding: In Wason's task people see the triple 2-4-6, are told it fits a hidden rule, propose triples and get yes or no. The true rule was any increasing sequence. People tended to test triples that fit their narrow guess (such as even numbers going up by two) and so could not learn the rule was broader. Jhaveri et al. quantify disconfirmatory testing as the ratio of incompatible to compatible tests (I:C).
numbers: 29 participants; 6 of 29 announced the right rule first time; 21 of 29 eventually found it. Mean I:C was 1.79 for first-time-correct vs 0.24 for first-time-wrong. Among first-wrong, second-correct had I:C 0.50 vs 0.19 for the rest.
limits: Wason's numbers as restated in a 2026 paper; Wason 1960 itself was not opened. The reading that people only confirm was later qualified by Klayman and Ha (a10).
agent_relevance: Human baseline for S7 counterexample search. Even people who found the rule mostly did not test against their hypothesis at the first announcement.

source: Klayman and Ha (1987) positive test strategy, as stated in Bertolazzi et al. (2026) and Batista and Griffiths (2026)
finding: Klayman and Ha separated positive testing (seek cases the hypothesis predicts will fit) from negative testing, and showed positive testing is not always bad. It can falsify a hypothesis H that is broader than the true rule R, but it cannot falsify H when H is a strict subset of R. Only then are negative tests needed. Positive testing is close to optimal when the target phenomenon is rare.
numbers: Set relations H vs R: if H is a strict subset of R only tests outside H can falsify; if H is a superset of R positive tests can falsify. Table 1 of Bertolazzi et al. lists all five cases.
limits: Second-hand statement of the 1987 paper (Psychological Review 94:211); the original was not opened (no open PDF found). Normative claim, not an effect size.
agent_relevance: Refines the schema line that people and models prefer confirming tests. The harmful case is a narrow hypothesis inside a broad rule. S7 could choose a negative test only when the current hypothesis may be too narrow, which code can check by listing where candidate rules differ.

source: Bertolazzi, Tentori and Bernardi (2026) FalsifyBench: rule discovery games for LLMs
finding: Generalised Wason 2-4-6 to semantic categories from WordNet: given three items from a narrow category (such as vertebrate), find the broader hidden category (animal) by proposing test triples and guessing. 100 games, 5 domains, 12 LLMs, max 20 turns, each model also acts as the oracle. Reasoning models do better and use far less confirmation. Success rises as the share of confirming tests falls.
numbers: Best instruction-tuned model DeepSeek-V3.1 41% success; GPT-5.2-Chat 75%; GPT-OSS-120B 68%; other instruction-tuned 33-35%; GPT-5-Nano 12%; Qwen3.5-9B 21%. Confirmation bias (share of confirming tests): instruction-tuned 66-82%; GPT-5-Mini 39.0%, GPT-5.2-Chat 27.3%, GPT-OSS-20B 24.2%. Spearman rho between success and confirmation bias = -0.779, p = 0.003 (12 models).
limits: Oracle errors do not explain it: Bayesian mixed-effects logistic regression on 1,200 games gave confirmation bias coefficient -4.15 (OR 0.016) and oracle error -0.12 with interval spanning zero. Small reasoning models did worse than all instruct models. Each model is its own oracle; GPT-5-Mini labels the H-R relation.
agent_relevance: Failure is in test choice, not knowledge. A program can count confirming vs falsifying tests and force a negative test when the hypothesis is probably too narrow.

source: Jhaveri, GX-Chen, Sucholutsky and Choi (2026) Failing to Falsify: confirmation bias in LLMs
finding: Wason-style rule discovery on 11 LLMs with a 45-turn limit. Models show confirmation bias, and less incompatible-to-compatible testing goes with slower and rarer success. Two human-derived fixes, Dual-Goal (name two rules, DAX and its complement MED) and Think-in-Opposites, raised success on average. Fine-tuning on intervention behaviour (distillation) generalised to a Blicket test.
numbers: Success ranged 6% to 78% across models. Counterexample-style prompts raised rule discovery from 42% to 56% on average. Think-in-Opposites improved success in all 11 model-by-mode cases; Dual-Goal in 8 of 11; I:C rose in 18 of 22 cases. Gemini-2.5-Pro: baseline 0.73, TiO 0.78, Dual-Goal 0.78. Qwen3-32B non-thinking baseline 0.33, TiO 0.36, Dual-Goal 0.10. 80 episodes per point.
limits: Gains significant for thinking models; mixed for non-thinking (Dual-Goal lowered Qwen3-32B non-thinking from 0.33 to 0.10 and Qwen3-14B from 0.23 to 0.13). Switching on thinking mode raised success without a steady rise in I:C, so thinking helps by another route. LLM judge reads the guesses.
agent_relevance: Source of the schema's 42% to 56% figure. Prompt framing helps some models and hurts others, so the S7 counterexample step needs a per-model test (G7) and is better run as code than as a prompt.

source: Banatt, Cheng, Vaidyanath and Hwu (2024) WILT: Wason Inductive Logic Test
finding: Multi-turn benchmark: a hidden boolean rule over 3 numbers (Python lambda); the model may pose up to 30 test triples and then guess once. 50 tasks per model. Best model got 14 of 50. Models differ in whether they are better at choosing tests (narrowing the hypothesis space) or at deducing the rule.
numbers: Claude 3.5 Sonnet 14/50 (28%); o1-mini 13/50; o1-preview 12/50; chatgpt-4o-latest 11/50; GPT-4o (2024-08-06) 9/50; Llama 3.1 405B 8/50; Claude 3 Haiku 1/50; Gemini 1.5 Flash 8b 0/50.
limits: Small N (50). Rules are written by the authors and may be harder than Wason's. Authors report that combining two models in the loop may beat one strong model.
agent_relevance: Splits the loop into pick-good-tests (E-space) and infer-rule (H-space), which fits keeping them as separate slots in S3 and S4.

source: Batista and Griffiths (2026) A Rational Analysis of the Effects of Sycophantic AI
finding: Human experiment with an AI chat partner on a modified 2-4-6 task (true rule: all three numbers even). A Bayesian analysis predicts that evidence sampled from your own hypothesis raises confidence but not accuracy. Default GPT-5.1 behaved like a confirming partner.
numbers: N = 557 (Prolific), 504 gave a final hypothesis. Discovery rate: random-sequence control 29.5%; rule-disconfirming 14.1%; agreeable 11.8%; rule-confirming 8.4%; default GPT 5.9%. Chi-square(4) = 28.02, p < .001. Default GPT vs random: diff 23.6 points, 95% CI -34.0 to -13.2. Rule-confirming vs rule-disconfirming 8.4 vs 14.1, p = .143 (not significant).
limits: Single true rule, three rounds, one model (GPT-5.1-Chat). The confirming vs disconfirming difference was not significant. Positive tests are uninformative by design here.
agent_relevance: A partner that answers from your hypothesis harms discovery. Supports G4, G9 and the rule that a judge sees no proposed answer (G5).

source: Jansen et al. (2024) DiscoveryWorld: virtual environment for automated scientific discovery agents
finding: Text world with 120 tasks across 8 topics (proteomics, chemistry, archaeology, reactor lab, plant nutrients, space sickness, rocket science, translation), 3 difficulty levels, 5 parametric seeds. Three baseline agents: ReAct, Plan+Execute and Hypothesizer (explicit hypothesis memory, CLIN-like). Scores: task completion, task process, explanatory knowledge.
numbers: Completion, easy / normal / challenge: ReAct 0.38 / 0.18 / 0.18; Plan+Execute 0.18 / 0.18 / 0.15; Hypothesizer 0.28 / 0.23 / 0.08. Knowledge discovered: ReAct 0.25 / 0.14 / 0.10; Plan+Execute 0.11 / 0.02 / 0.01; Hypothesizer 0.34 / 0.19 / 0.08. Human scientists (MSc or PhD, Upwork): 66% mean completion, 55% knowledge, 11 of 16 tasks over 60%.
limits: Baseline LLM of 2024; easy tasks capped at 100 steps, others 1000. Humans did 16 tasks only. Unit-test tasks (single skills) had completion above 60%, so parts work and the whole loop fails.
agent_relevance: Explicit hypothesis memory (Hypothesizer) raised knowledge on easy tasks but not completion, and fell on challenge tasks. A hypothesis list alone does not give discovery; the agent also needs experiment choice that targets unexplained results (see a21).

source: Wang et al. (2023) Hypothesis Search: inductive reasoning with language models
finding: Pipeline: GPT-4 writes 64 natural-language hypotheses, summarises to 8, writes programs from each, and checks the programs on the examples with up to 3 rounds of execution feedback. On 100 random ARC tasks it lifted accuracy; correct hypothesis generation was the bottleneck.
numbers: ARC (100 tasks, top-1): direct prompting 17%; program only 23%; summarised hypotheses 30%; human-selected hypotheses 33%; human-written hypotheses 45%; Icecuber (non-LLM DSL) 43%. GPT-4 produced a correct hypothesis for only 49 tasks; of those 49, 33 (67%) gave correct programs. Of 30 solved via summarised hypotheses, 28 had a correct hypothesis before summarising. SyGuS: 94.3% with 4 hypotheses x 2 programs vs 74.8% for CrossBeam. 1D-ARC: program-only 61.1%.
limits: GPT-4 (2023), top-1 rather than the official top-3 scoring. Human-written hypotheses came from LARC annotations. Programs are tested on the given examples only.
agent_relevance: Closest published match to S3 plus S4: many hypotheses, a code test, execution feedback. The gap from 30% to 45% shows hypothesis quality, not program writing, is the limit. Also G3: passing the given examples is not proof.

source: Shojaee et al. (2025) LLM-SR: scientific equation discovery via programming with LLMs
finding: Treats equations as programs with free parameters. The LLM proposes equation skeletons using domain knowledge, a numeric optimiser fits the parameters, and an experience buffer of best programs feeds the next round. Compared with symbolic regression (GPlearn, E2E, DSR, uDSR, PySR) on four problems in-domain (ID) and out-of-domain (OOD).
numbers: Backbones GPT-3.5-turbo and Mixtral-8x7B. NMSE for LLM-SR was lower by orders of magnitude on the oscillators, for example Oscillation 1 about 1e-7 to 1e-8 in-domain vs about 3e-4 to 1e-2 for baselines (table text garbled in extraction; check the paper). Ablations on Oscillation 2: removing the prior, the program form, or iterative refinement each hurt.
limits: Four problems, two of them custom synthetic oscillators built to avoid LLM recitation. Some real-data cells (E. coli growth) look worse than baselines. Numbers read from a garbled table.
agent_relevance: BACON-style search over term forms, now with an LLM proposing the form and code fitting the parameters. Fits 'model fills a slot, program decides' and shows an OOD check acting as G3.

source: Si, Yang and Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs Generate Novel Research Ideas? A large-scale human study
finding: Blind review of expert-written ideas vs LLM ideas on NLP topics. LLM ideas were rated more novel. LLM ideation lacked diversity and LLM-as-judge was unreliable.
numbers: 79 expert reviewers, 49 ideas per condition. Novelty mean: human 4.84, AI 5.64, AI plus human rerank 5.81 (p < 0.05, Welch's t-test with multiple-test correction). Of 4,000 generated seed ideas per topic only about 200 were non-duplicates (cosine similarity above 0.8). Best LLM judge reached 53.3% accuracy at ranking top vs bottom 25%, below human inter-reviewer consistency of 56.1%; GPT-4o direct 50.0%, GPT-4o pairwise 45.0%, Claude-3.5 direct 51.7%.
limits: Novelty is a judgement, not an executed result (the authors propose a follow-up in which people execute the ideas). Human ideas were written under time limits.
agent_relevance: Supports G8 (do not let a model judge novelty) and the open-mode rule of tracking directions tried, since duplicates saturate quickly.

source: Lu et al. (2024) The AI Scientist: fully automated open-ended scientific discovery
finding: End-to-end pipeline: idea generation, code edits with Aider, experiment runs with up to four retries, plotting, paper writing, automated review. Cost under 15 dollars per paper. Authors list failure modes: many ideas cannot be implemented, wrong implementations are hard to catch, too few experiments for fair controls, occasional hallucinated results.
numbers: Automated reviewer: 65% vs 66% balanced accuracy for human NeurIPS reviewers, AUC 0.65 for both, on ICLR 2022 OpenReview data. Under 15 dollars per paper.
limits: Reviewer score is against accept/reject labels, not truth. Authors state limited experiments often lead to deceptive or inaccurate conclusions. An early version hallucinated an entire ablations table.
agent_relevance: A generate-test loop with an LLM reviewer produces fluent but unchecked claims. Supports G2, G3 and G10 (do not trust the write-up).

source: Jansen et al. (2024) DiscoveryWorld: agents handle single steps, not the whole loop
finding: Agents manage single steps such as measuring objects with instruments (unit-test tasks, completion above 60%) but fail at end-to-end discovery.
numbers: Humans 66% completion; best agent on challenge tasks 18% completion (ReAct) and 8% knowledge (Hypothesizer). Authors' reading: agents lack the capacity for end-to-end discovery in most settings.
limits: Different step budgets for easy (100) vs normal and challenge (1000). Same paper as a15.
agent_relevance: The weak part is control between hypothesis and experiment work, not any single operator. The schema's program-owned transitions are meant to supply that control.

source: Joshi, Shethia and Lam (2026) SHELDON: reasoning through dual search over hypothesis and observation spaces
finding: Builds a harness directly from Klahr and Dunbar's dual-space idea. It keeps hypotheses and observations as separate stored objects linked by evidence relations, and seeks observations that no current hypothesis explains. Beats evaluated baselines on diagnosis, ARC-AGI-2 and optimisation tasks.
numbers: Up to 26.7 points over baselines. DiagnosisArena 84.00 (RLM 78.00, Codex 76.00); ORCA-Bench 66.67 vs best baseline 40.00; ARC-AGI-2 59.17 vs EvoX 47.50 at a 2.5 dollar budget per task; QNN topology 1.00 vs 0.85 best agent. Ablation (DiagnosisArena / ORCA / ARC / QNN): without comparative analysis 78.00 / 56.67 / 50.00 / 0.883; without observation space 70.00 / 53.33 / 50.00 / 0.867; without continued exploration 82.00 / 53.33 / 57.70 / 0.733. Of 782 ARC hypotheses born after round 1, 204 cite an observation in the rationale (158 from testing a different hypothesis).
limits: Preprint (Oct 2026) with the authors' own task selection and small task counts; no independent replication. Baselines are proprietary agents run at different budgets.
agent_relevance: Strongest recent test of the two-space idea. The observation-space ablation is the cleanest evidence that storing and seeking unexplained observations pays. Candidate refinement of S4 and S7; check G7 before adding.

source: Gandhi et al. (2025) BoxingGym: automated experimental design and model discovery
finding: 10 environments built as generative probabilistic models (psychology to ecology). Experiment quality is measured by expected information gain regret (EIG regret) against the best of 100 random experiments, and model quality by whether the agent's explanation helps another agent predict. Larger models help; prior knowledge in the prompt often does not.
numbers: 5 runs, 10 evaluation points. 32B models beat 7B within a family. Instruction-tuned Qwen2.5 outperformed reasoning-tuned OpenThinker. GPT-4o had lowest EIG regret. With domain context removed, models often did as well or better after 10 experiments. In hyperbolic discounting, error rose with more experiments. Box's Apprentice (LM plus statistical model fitting) did not reliably beat plain GPT-4o.
limits: Open and closed models of 2025 size; standard errors across 5 runs only. Prior effect was environment-specific.
agent_relevance: Prior knowledge can lock in a wrong model (the agent does not revise an early assumption). Supports G1 and G2: revise from real output, and treat rising error with more data as a signal to recheck.

source: Wang et al. (2022) ScienceWorld: is your agent smarter than a 5th grader?
finding: Interactive text benchmark of 30 elementary-science tasks. Models answer what a known material's conductivity is but fail to run an experiment to find an unknown one. A 1.5 million parameter DRRN agent was competitive with much larger language-model agents.
numbers: Best normalised average score 0.17 across tasks, similar to medium-difficulty interactive fiction (Zork-like).
limits: 2022 text agents, not current LLMs; not an explicit two-space design.
agent_relevance: Early evidence that knowing a fact and running the experiment that finds it are different skills. Background only.

source: Majumder et al. (2024) DiscoveryBench: data-driven discovery with LLMs
finding: Benchmark of data-driven discovery goals (find a hypothesis from datasets). The best system solves a quarter of tasks.
numbers: Best agent 25% (abstract and discussion text read).
limits: Only the headline number and abstract were checked; framework details not read.
agent_relevance: Context number: the full loop of finding a hypothesis from data is still weak.

source: Chen et al. (2025) ScienceAgentBench: language agents for data-driven scientific discovery
finding: Tasks drawn from peer-reviewed papers; agents write programs. The best agent solves under a third of tasks.
numbers: Best agent 32.4% independently, 34.3% with expert-provided knowledge (three attempts per task); OpenAI o1 also tested with direct prompting and self-debug.
limits: Only the abstract and introduction lines were read. Success is program execution against a gold output, not discovery of new knowledge.
agent_relevance: A code check exists for these tasks, yet agents solve a third, so the limit is hypothesis and plan quality, not lack of a check.

source: Fa and Culjak (2026) Sound Agentic Science Requires Adversarial Experiments
finding: Position paper (ICLR 2026 workshop): agents make endlessly revisable analyses, so the hypothesis space becomes candidate claims propped up by chosen analyses. It proposes a falsification-first standard: use agents to search for ways a claim can fail.
numbers: No measured results in the abstract and introduction read.
limits: Position paper with no experiment. Only abstract and introduction were read.
agent_relevance: Matches the schema's bias toward counterexample search (S7) and G3.

source: Yuh et al. (2026) Bayesian Model Discovery with Language Models
finding: Closes the loop: an LLM proposes model families, a numeric engine fits parameters and scores them by model evidence, and the next experiment is chosen by expected information gain over families and parameters; residual diagnostics return to the LLM. Beats in-context learning and LLM scientist agents on four benchmarks.
numbers: Four benchmarks; lower final prediction error and more exact functional forms recovered than ICL and agents. Ablations support numerical feedback and the joint objective. Exact numbers not read.
limits: Only the abstract and introduction were read; effect sizes are not recorded here.
agent_relevance: Pairs with SHELDON: choose experiments by computed information gain, not by the model's taste. Fits 'code selects' (G5).

source: Klahr and Dunbar (1988) Dual Space Search During Scientific Reasoning, Cognitive Science 12:1-48 (original paper)
finding: Original SDDS paper. Not opened: the Wiley PDF returned HTTP 403 and no open copy was found. Facts about it in a01 to a05 come from Klahr 1994, read this session.
numbers: Semantic Scholar metadata lists 1,189 citations (metadata only).
limits: Do not cite exact N or percentages from the 1988 paper until it is read.
agent_relevance: Open item: obtain the paper to extract exact adult and child counts, the Theorist/Experimenter split and confirming vs disconfirming test counts.

source: Klahr and Simon (1999) Studies of Scientific Discovery: Complementary Approaches and Convergent Findings, Psychological Bulletin 125:524
finding: Review linking psychological studies and BACON-style computer discovery systems. Not opened: the APA page needs a login and no open PDF was found.
numbers: Semantic Scholar metadata only: 342 citations.
limits: Content not read.
agent_relevance: Open item: read for convergence claims between human data and discovery programs.
